numbers.headline: Of 530 Americans ever hooked on weed, 344 were already free of it when they were interviewed.
numbers.mirror: You think being hooked on weed is just who you are now.
numbers.counted: people who had ever been hooked on weed

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews, one snapshot
basis.who: US adults who had ever met the older DSM-IV criteria for dependence on weed (3 or more of 7 signs within a year)
basis.n: 530 adults ever hooked on weed (of 43,093 surveyed); 344 of them were free by the interview
basis.measured: Whether the signs of being hooked had finally stopped and never come back, as people recalled it. Free here means no signs of being hooked any more; it does not have to mean never using.

numbers.caveat: 344 of 530 is about 65%, a raw head count before the survey's weighting. Some of the other 186 may still get free later. The authors say people may over-report getting free, and people in prison or hospital weren't asked. Weed was weaker in 2001 than today.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction.

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/cannabis.json who '6 years' (its head count, 344 of 530; refetched from PMC on 2026-11-05)

numbers.headline: 97% of Americans ever hooked on weed are projected to get free of it at some point in their lives.
numbers.mirror: You think you've smoked too long to ever get free.
numbers.counted: people who had ever been hooked on weed

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews; ages recalled, then a statistical model projects the share over a whole life
basis.who: US adults who had ever met the older DSM-IV criteria for dependence on weed
basis.n: 530 adults ever hooked on weed (of 43,093 surveyed)
basis.measured: The age when the signs of being hooked first appeared and the age when they finally stopped and never came back, as recalled. From these ages the model projects the share free by the end of life. A projected 66% were free within 10 years.

numbers.caveat: A model, not a head count: 344 of the 530 were free when asked. People in prison or hospital weren't surveyed, so the authors say the true share is probably lower. Free means no signs of being hooked, not never using. Men got free more slowly than women.
numbers.weak: A projection from recalled ages that likely runs high; the same paper's projections for each ethnic group run from 82% to 96%, all below 97%.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction.
ref.quote: Lifetime cumulative probability estimates of dependence remission were … 97.2% for cannabis

numbers.headline: Americans who beat a weed problem were about 29, on average, when it ended.
numbers.mirror: You're in your twenties and fear you'll never stop.
numbers.counted: people who beat a weed problem

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey), one snapshot, answered online
basis.who: US adults who said they used to have a substance problem but no longer do, and named weed as the main one. Many also had a past problem with another substance.
basis.n: About 217 people whose main problem was weed (a weighted count, of 2,002)
basis.measured: Age when the problem ended, as people remembered it. On average they started weekly use at about 17 and the problem lasted about 12 years.

numbers.caveat: An average age, not a cut-off: the likely range for the average is about 26 to 31. It counts only people who said they got free. The problem was their own judgment: in the whole survey only about 1 in 6 had ever been diagnosed.
numbers.weak: The problem was self-defined and most in this survey were never diagnosed, so milder cases are mixed in with addiction.

ref.cite: Kelly JF, Greene MC, Bergman BG (2018). Is recovery from cannabis use problems different from alcohol and other drugs? Results from a national probability-based sample of the United States adult population. International Journal of Drug Policy.
ref.quote: The average age at problem resolution was also significantly younger for CAN (M = 28.87 years; 99% CI: 26.46, 31.29)

numbers.headline: About 54% of Americans who beat a weed problem never used treatment, a group or medicine.
numbers.mirror: You think you can't get off weed without rehab.
numbers.counted: people who beat a weed problem

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey), one snapshot, answered online
basis.who: US adults who said they used to have a substance problem but no longer do, and named weed as the main one. Many also had a past problem with another substance.
basis.n: About 220 people whose main problem was weed (11% of a weighted 2,002)
basis.measured: Ever used, at any point: mutual-help groups (such as Marijuana Anonymous), outpatient or inpatient treatment, anti-craving medicine, or recovery services such as sober living. 45.8% had used one or more; the other 54% used none.

numbers.caveat: Help could be one meeting or years of treatment. It doesn't show which route worked better; people with worse problems used help more. About 220 people, so the true share could be several points either way. The problem was their own judgment: in the whole survey only about 1 in 6 had ever been diagnosed.
numbers.weak: The problem was self-defined and most in this survey were never diagnosed, so milder cases are mixed in with addiction.

ref.cite: Kelly JF, Bergman B, Hoeppner BB, Vilsaint C, White WL (2017). Prevalence and pathways of recovery from drug and alcohol problems in the United States population: implications for practice, research, and policy. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.

numbers.headline: Half of Americans who beat a weed problem needed 2 serious tries or fewer.
numbers.mirror: You've tried to stop before and think you've failed for good.
numbers.counted: people who beat a weed problem

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey), one snapshot, answered online
basis.who: US adults who said they used to have a substance problem but no longer do, and named weed as the main one. Many also had a past problem with another substance.
basis.n: About 217 people whose main problem was weed (a weighted count, of 2,002)
basis.measured: Number of serious tries before the problem was resolved, as people remembered it, counting everyone, including people who never needed a serious try. The middle half needed 1 to 4.

numbers.caveat: Counts only people who succeeded, from memory. The average was higher, about 5, because a few needed many. The question asked about tries before they overcame it, so some may not have counted the try that worked. The problem was their own judgment: in the whole survey only about 1 in 6 had ever been diagnosed.
numbers.weak: The problem was self-defined and most in this survey were never diagnosed, so milder cases are mixed in with addiction.

ref.cite: Kelly JF, Greene MC, Bergman BG, White WL, Hoeppner BB (2019). How many recovery attempts does it take to successfully resolve an alcohol or drug problem? Estimates and correlates from a national study of recovering U.S. adults. Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research.

numbers.headline: Of daily users changing on their own, 85% tried cutting down; only 8% later had a month without weed.
numbers.mirror: You keep cutting down instead of stopping, and it never lasts.
numbers.counted: daily weed users trying to stop or cut down alone

basis.design: daily phone check-ins for 3 months, then a survey at 6 months
basis.who: daily or near-daily weed users (5+ days a week) planning to stop or cut down on their own, not in treatment; half men, average age 32. 75% met the checklist for a weed problem, mild cases included.
basis.measured: Each day: weed use, and whether they were trying to stop or cut down. 85% tried cutting down at some point and 46% tried stopping. At 6 months, 8% had not used weed in the last month.

numbers.caveat: Volunteers paid for daily calls, not a random sample. Almost every try to stop or cut down lasted under a week. Only 6% sought treatment. More days of cutting down or stopping went with fewer signs of being hooked later. It does not show that cutting down works better or worse than stopping.
numbers.weak: Daily users, not all checked as hooked (a quarter did not meet the checklist), and paid volunteers.

ref.cite: Hughes JR, Naud S, Budney AJ, Fingar JR, Callas PW (2016). Attempts to stop or reduce daily cannabis use: an intensive natural history study. Psychology of Addictive Behaviors.
ref.quote: Most (85%) participants made an intentional reduction attempt during the study.

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/cannabis.json how '85%' (figure, n and ref kept; 75%-met-checklist and the 8% line added from the refetched PMC full text, 2026-11-05; not picked in kinds.json, included because a checked number exists)

numbers.headline: Of people treated for weed who got two weeks off, 71% slipped at least once within 6 months.
numbers.mirror: You slipped once and think the whole quit is ruined.
numbers.counted: people in treatment for weed who got two weeks off

basis.design: follow-up of an outpatient treatment group
basis.who: adults in outpatient treatment for marijuana dependence who reached at least 2 weeks without weed
basis.measured: First use of any weed (a slip), and return to heavier use (4+ days in any 7 days), over 6 months. On average the first slip came about 73 days in.

numbers.caveat: A slip is common, not the end of a try. But 71% of those who slipped went back to heavier use, and early slips were riskier.
numbers.weak: Only 82 people from one treatment programme, studied over 20 years ago.

ref.cite: Moore BA, Budney AJ (2003). Relapse in outpatient treatment for marijuana dependence. Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment.
ref.quote: Seventy-one percent used marijuana at least once (i.e., lapsed) within 6 months of initial abstinence, averaging 73 days (SD = 50) till lapsing.

numbers.headline: 63% of Americans who beat a weed problem no longer used it at all; about 1 in 3 still used some.
numbers.mirror: You hope you can keep smoking now and then, just not daily.
numbers.counted: people who beat a weed problem

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey), one snapshot, answered online
basis.who: US adults who said they used to have a substance problem but no longer do, and named weed as the main one. Many also had a past problem with another substance.
basis.n: About 217 people whose main problem was weed (a weighted count, of 2,002)
basis.measured: Whether people were abstinent from weed at the time of the survey, among those who said the problem was over.

numbers.caveat: It shows which way people who got free went, not which way works better. They judged for themselves that the problem was over. It doesn't say how much the 1 in 3 still use, or how many tried to keep using and slid back. The problem was their own judgment: in the whole survey only about 1 in 6 had ever been diagnosed.
numbers.weak: Counts only people who got free, so it cannot compare how often stopping and cutting down fail; the problem was self-defined.

numbers.headline: No medicine is approved to help people quit weed; in trials, THC-based pills and NAC worked no better than dummy pills.
numbers.mirror: You've hoped a doctor could give you a pill to quit.
numbers.counted: people hooked on weed in medicine trials

basis.who: people diagnosed as hooked on weed, or likely to be; mostly adults, and most trials were mostly men
basis.n: 3,201 people in 37 trials (THC medicines: 290 people in 4 trials; NAC: 270 in 2)
basis.where: mostly USA (29 trials), also Australia, Israel, Canada and the UK
basis.measured: Being off weed at the end of treatment, medicine against a dummy pill. CBD and anti-seizure medicines had too little testing to tell.

numbers.caveat: Not proof that pills can't help: most were tested in few, small trials, and the review calls the evidence uncertain. Because no medicine beat a dummy pill, there is no '1 in N' figure yet.

ref.cite: Spiga F, Parkhouse T, Tang VM, Savović J, Le Foll B, Nielsen S (2025). Pharmacotherapies for cannabis use disorder. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: There are currently no pharmacotherapies approved for the treatment of cannabis use disorder

numbers.headline: In 23 trials of talk therapy for weed, about 1 in 4 people were off weed at the last check-up.
numbers.mirror: You wonder if therapy is worth it after failing alone.
numbers.counted: people in therapy trials for a weed problem

basis.who: adults with a weed problem (cannabis use disorder), treated as outpatients or in the community
basis.where: 15 trials in the USA; others in Australia, Germany, Switzerland, Canada, Brazil and Ireland
basis.measured: Weed use, being off weed, and signs of being hooked, against minimal or no treatment; about 7 sessions over 12 weeks. More than 4 sessions over more than a month did better. Adding rewards (vouchers for weed-free urine tests) helped in 5 of 6 trials.

numbers.caveat: At around 4 months, therapy made people about 2.5 times as likely to say they weren't using, but that evidence is weak. No kind of therapy clearly worked at 9 months or later. The 1 in 4 is a rough share across trials, not the gain over doing nothing.

ref.cite: Gates PJ, Sabioni P, Copeland J, Le Foll B, Gowing L (2016). Psychosocial interventions for cannabis use disorder. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: abstinence rates were relatively low overall, with approximately one-quarter of participants abstinent at final follow-up.

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/cannabis.json works '1 in 4' (figure, basis and ref kept; abstract refetched from Europe PMC on 2026-11-05)

numbers.headline: Young regular users who stopped for a month got better at learning and remembering words, mostly in the first week.
numbers.mirror: You feel foggy and fear your memory won't come back.
numbers.counted: regular weed users aged 16 to 25, not checked for addiction

basis.design: randomised study: 4 weeks off weed vs. carry on using
basis.who: regular users aged 16–25 from the community and a high school, using on about 55 of the last 90 days
basis.n: 62 asked to stop for a month, with rewards for clean urine tests, vs 26 who kept using (55 stayed off all 30 days)
basis.measured: memory and attention tests at the start and every week for 4 weeks

numbers.caveat: Memory improved; attention did not. Young users only, and not checked for addiction. It could not say whether school or work results improved.
numbers.weak: A small trial (62 who stopped) of young users who were not checked for addiction.

ref.cite: Schuster RM, Gilman J, Schoenfeld D, et al. (2018). One month of cannabis abstinence in adolescents and young adults is associated with improved memory. Journal of Clinical Psychiatry.
ref.quote: There was an effect of abstinence on verbal memory (P = .002) ... driven by improved verbal learning in the first week of abstinence.

numbers.headline: In a 12-week trial for a weed problem, people who cut down grew less anxious and less depressed, and slept better.

numbers.counted: adults in a treatment trial for a weed problem

basis.design: follow-up inside a 12-week medicine trial (secondary analysis)
basis.who: adults aged 18–50 in a trial for cannabis use disorder
basis.n: 302 adults (152 whose use went down, 150 whose use went up)
basis.measured: changes in anxiety, depression, sleep quality and quality of life, next to changes in weed use

gaps.note: Filled with 63% (people who beat a weed problem who no longer use it), which shows the route taken, not which route works. No study was found that compares relapse after stopping with relapse after cutting down among people who had been hooked on weed (the kind of figure the alcohol page's '27% vs 7%' gives).
gaps.searched: Europe PMC: cannabis/marijuana + remission/recurrence/persistence + abstinence/non-abstinent/moderation/controlled use; cannabis quit vs reduce. Seen: Lozano 2006 (Addiction, PMID 17034438, 291 treatment-seekers; people reached the goal they picked, abstract has no figures, full text paywalled), Stea 2015 (PMID 26168224, 119 recovered; abstinent recoveries had worse histories, no figures in abstract), Brezing 2018 (PMC5846101, 62 people, quality of life, no simple figure), Levin 2021 (PMC8282674, trial reduction categories, no stop-vs-cut figure), Farmer 2015 (PMC4229487, recurrence 27.7% but not split by continued use), Hughes 2016 (daily users, tag 'heavy', not allowed in the helps group; used under how-abrupt).
gaps.later: Our r/leaves harvest already counts relapse posts by day (103 of 221 after more than a month off; 'I can moderate now' named most). A count of moderation-try posts and how they ended could fill this later as a self-hooked number.

gaps.note: No medicine beat a dummy pill for being off weed (Cochrane 2025), so the '1 in N' form the kind asks for does not exist. Shown as '0 pills'.
gaps.searched: Cochrane 2025 (PMID 41025421) abstract refetched; no single trial was taken over the review.
